nameStory: The four-toed salamander gets its name from a unique feature among salamanders - it has only four toes on its back feet, while most salamanders have five. This distinctive trait makes it instantly recognizable once you know what to look for. The scientific name Hemidactylium literally means "half finger," referring to this reduced number of digits.
description: The four-toed salamander is a small, delicate lungless salamander that's truly one of New England's most distinctive amphibians. Adults typically reach 2.5-4 inches in total length, with about half of that being their remarkably thin tail. They have a golden-brown to reddish-brown back with fine dark speckling, a bright white belly often marked with black spots, and that telltale constriction where the tail meets the body that looks almost like a rubber band was tied around it.

idTips.label: Toes
idTips.description: Only four toes on the hind feet instead of the usual five - count carefully with a magnifying glass or close photo, as this is the definitive field mark

idTips.label: Tail Constriction
idTips.description: Deep groove where tail meets body creates a pinched appearance, like a twist-tie marking - the tail feels almost detached when gently handled

idTips.label: Color/Pattern
idTips.description: Warm golden-brown to rusty-red back with fine dark pepper-like specks, contrasting sharply with a bright white or cream belly that may have bold black spots

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny and thread-like - adults fit easily on a quarter, with an extremely thin tail that makes up about half their total length

idTips.label: Skin
idTips.description: Smooth, moist skin that feels slightly sticky to the touch, typical of lungless salamanders but more delicate than most

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found near sphagnum moss bogs or acidic wetlands - if you're not in boggy habitat, you're probably looking at a different species

habitat: Four-toed salamanders are specialists of acidic, boggy environments throughout New England's lowlands and mountains. Look for them under logs, moss mats, and leaf litter near sphagnum bogs, cedar swamps, and the marshy edges of acidic ponds. They're particularly associated with areas where sphagnum moss forms thick, spongy carpets that stay consistently moist.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and migrate to bog edges for breeding. This is the best time to find them active near water, often under logs or moss near their breeding pools.
seasonality.summer: Eggs hatch and tiny larvae develop in acidic pools while adults retreat deeper into moss mats and underground. Surface sightings become less common as they avoid hot, dry conditions.
seasonality.fall: Juvenile salamanders complete metamorphosis and adults may be found again under surface cover as they prepare for winter. Cool, moist days offer the best viewing opportunities.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep in moss, under logs, or underground below the frost line. Virtually impossible to find during this dormant period.

funFact: Four-toed salamanders can deliberately break off their tail at that constricted groove when grabbed by a predator - and unlike lizards, they can actually grow it back perfectly, complete with the same constriction pattern!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with young red-backed salamanders, but remember: count the toes and look for that pinched waist where the tail meets the body. Red-backed salamanders have five toes on all feet and no tail constriction. If you're not in boggy habitat, it's almost certainly not a four-toed salamander.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name suggesting they're missing a toe, four-toed salamanders actually represent an evolutionary reduction rather than a loss - this is their natural state. The species is the sole member of its genus, making it quite unique in the salamander world.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus, the four-toed salamander is truly unique among New England salamanders. Its closest relatives in the lungless salamander family include red-backed salamanders and two-lined salamanders, but neither shares the four-toed trait or the dramatic tail constriction. The combination of bog habitat, four rear toes, and that pinched tail base makes this species unmistakable once you know what to look for.
